title: Generating Assessments
answer: Generating assessments covers the creation of quiz questions, test items, rubrics, and distractors from course materials and stated learning objectives. The work spans formative checks, summative exams, practice banks, and competency based tasks across many subjects and levels. Outputs include multiple choice, short answer, matching, scenario based, and performance task prompts. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Generating assessments covers the creation of quiz questions, test items, rubrics, and distractors from course materials and stated learning objectives. The work spans formative checks, summative exams, practice banks, and competency based tasks across many subjects and levels. Outputs include multiple choice, short answer, matching, scenario based, and performance task prompts. The goal is to produce items that measure the intended knowledge or skill rather than surface recall alone.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most generation runs on large language models accessed through an application programming interface or a local model. The system typically takes source texts such as syllabi, lecture notes, textbooks, or item specifications as input. Some setups use retrieval augmented generation to ground questions in a specific document set. Results are often delivered into a learning management system or a question bank file for instructor review.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A course designer or teacher supplies the learning objective, the source material, and the desired item type and difficulty. The model is prompted to produce a stem, correct answer, and plausible distractors, often with a short rationale for each option. The instructor then reviews, edits, and approves items, checking alignment with the objective and the level of cognitive demand. Iteration is common, with feedback used to refine wording, remove ambiguity, and adjust difficulty.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk questions center on the provenance of source materials, the originality of generated items, and the privacy of student or course data. Bias can enter through training data or poorly written prompts, so human review remains a standard control. Institutions often require that generated assessments be labeled as machine assisted and that instructors retain final authority over what is used. Accessibility standards and academic integrity policies also shape what may be deployed.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward assessments that adapt to a learner's responses and that are calibrated against item response theory or similar measurement models. Future systems may generate items with images, simulations, or interactive tasks, and align them more tightly to competency frameworks. Work is also moving toward automated quality checks for fairness, readability, and construct validity, with the teacher remaining the decision maker on final use.
